title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 278
paragraphs: To Heliopolis and Buto they go year by year and do sacrifice only; but at Papremis they do sacrifice and worship as elsewhere, and besides that, when the sun begins to go down, while a few of the priests are busy with the image of the god, the greater number of them stand at the entrance of the temple with wooden clubs; and other men, more than a thousand in number who have a vow to perform, stand in a body opposite, these too all with staves of wood. The image, which is in a small wooden shrine covered with gold, they take out on the day before to another sacred building. The few, then, who have been left about the image draw a wagon with four wheels that bears the shrine and the image within it, and the other priests standing in the gateway try to prevent it from entering, and the men under a vow come to the aid of the god and strike them, while the others defend themselves. Then there comes a hard fight with staves, and they break one another's heads; and I am of opinion that many even die of the wounds they receive — though the Egyptians told me that no one died. The people of the place say they established this solemn assembly for the following reason. The mother of Ares, they say, used to dwell in this temple; and Ares, having been brought up away from her, when he grew up came there desiring to visit his mother; but the attendants of his mother's temple, not having seen him before, did not permit him to pass in, and kept him away. He then brought men to help him from another city and handled the attendants of the temple roughly, and entered to visit his mother. Hence, they say, this exchange of blows has become the custom in honour of Ares at his festival.
